query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Simultaneous high‐rate laser calorimetry combined with in‐situ acoustic emission measurements can provide an integrated, accurate determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting across diverse high‐entropy alloy compositions. The acoustic signals, which correlate with rapid volumetric changes and non-ideal mixing in the liquid phase, will complement ultrafast DSC data so that, when coupled with iterative high‐throughput CALPHAD and machine‐learning refinements, the method achieves quantitative accuracies within ~5% compared to benchmark experiments.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk, homogenized HEA specimens (e.g., equiatomic or near-equiatomic alloys synthesized via arc melting) with well‐characterized microstructures and grain sizes.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled, laser‐induced rapid heating (with heating rates of 10^3–10^5 K/s) in a protective inert environment while simultaneously recording high‐resolution DSC (for heat flow) and acoustic emission signals (for detecting volume changes and phase transitions).
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere in a custom high-rate calorimetry setup with integrated high-sensitivity piezoelectric transducers. Temperature ranges span from room temperature to above the expected melting points (up to ~3000 K for refractory HEAs), with calibration provided by synchrotron X-ray diffraction or neutron imaging in select runs.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrated calorimetry–acoustic data capture the rapid thermodynamic and volumetric responses during the melting transition, including any multi‐stage (e.g., pre‐melting at grain boundaries) phenomena. These responses reflect the interplay of configurational, thermal, vibrational, and electronic entropy contributions as well as non-ideal mixing in the liquid state.
generation.mechanism: During laser heating, endothermic events from DSC identify fusion and phase-change temperatures while acoustic emissions register sudden volume changes associated with melting and liquid structural rearrangements. A machine-learning model iteratively refines CALPHAD predictions using these dual signals, separating contributions from different entropy sources and resolving potential two-stage melting processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will accurately determine melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume changes with an expected quantitative performance of ±5% compared to independent high-resolution DSC and in-situ diffraction benchmarks. In HEAs where MD simulations and conventional DSC have disagreed (e.g., showing either two-stage melting or a single-step transition), the added acoustic signature will decisively reveal the actual melting kinetics and volumetric expansion, thereby validating or ruling out simulation-only predictions.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC measurements and MD/MC simulation studies carried out separately (e.g., as reported in PMC7513177 and PMC8956691).
generation.boundary: The method applies to HEAs with melting points within the accessible range of current laser-based rapid heating systems (up to ~3000 K) and where acoustic emission signals are distinguishable from background noise; its performance on ultra-high melting systems or in alloys with extremely subtle volume changes remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: While individual DSC studies (PMC7513177::web::000::abstract) and MD simulations (PMC8956691::web::012::results_and_discussion) have provided insights into separate aspects of melting, the new proposal introduces in-situ acoustic measurements and a machine-learning–CALPHAD feedback loop to capture volumetric changes and disentangle entropy contributions. Uncertainty exists in integrating acoustic data with calorimetric signals and in the ML extrapolation across very different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples (spanning different compositions and grain sizes) and measure their melting curves using the proposed integrated laser-DSC/acoustic method. In parallel, perform independent high-resolution DSC and in-situ synchrotron/neutron imaging experiments to obtain benchmark melting temperatures, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change data. Compare the integrated method’s outputs with these benchmarks.
measurements: In-situ diffraction (XRD/neutron imaging) for structural confirmation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated method’s measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, or volume change deviates by more than 10% from the independently obtained benchmark values, or if the acoustic signals do not consistently correlate with structural changes observed by diffraction, then the proposed approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.3. Increase of Melting Temperature in HE-RE
cited_evidence.text: To raise the melting temperature, nonideality must favor the solid over the liquid. This can occur by one or both of the following: negative deviations from ideality in the solid phase or positive deviations in the liquid phase. Negative deviations in the solid solution are generally associated with local ordering, hinting at a tendency toward compound formation, and resulting in negative heats of mixing. The volumetric behavior described above shows no evidence for ordering, but volume is not necessarily a good proxy for energetics. The other possibility is strongly positive deviations from ideal mixing in the molten oxides, leading, in the extreme, to liquid–liquid phase separation. We know very little about the structure and thermodynamics of molten binary or multicomponent rare earth oxide systems, except for a recent report from Nakanishi and Allanore [] on non-ideal mixing in La2O3-Y2O3 melt, so this possible scenario cannot be assessed at present.

AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. The melting mechanism of single crystal and polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) were investigated by the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the second-nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) potential. For the single crystal RHEA, the density profile displays an abrupt drop from 11.25 to 11.00 g/cm3 at temperatures from 2910 to 2940 K, indicating all atoms begin significant local structural rearrangement. For polycrystalline RHEAs, a two-stage melting process is found. In the first melting stage, the melting of the grain boundary (GB) regions firstly occurs at the pre-melting temperature, which is relatively lower than the corresponding system-melting point. At the pre-melting temperature, most GB atoms have enough kinetic energies to leave their equilibrium positions, and then gradually induce the rearrangement of grain atoms close to GB. In the second melting stage at the melting point, most grain atoms have enough kinetic energies to rearrange, resulting in the chemical short-ranged order changes of all pairs.
